title: If Europe wants to use its trade leverage with China, now is the time
gist: MERICS customs-data analysis finds China depends on the EU for 110 HS6 product categories in 2024 versus just 56 for the US, and for 15 strategic categories versus only 3 from the US — so Europe retains real collective trade leverage. But that leverage is decaying fast (down from 225 categories in 2000, and Germany alone down to nine), which is why MERICS argues the window to use it is now, via a Commission-empowered Anti-Coercion Instrument, local sourcing rules and a Germany that finally aligns with a common EU strategy.

themes.theme: China's decaying dependence on EU imports

insights.claim: The number of product categories in which China ran a big trade deficit, relied on the EU for at least 30 percent of imports, and had limited alternative suppliers fell to 110 in 2024 from 225 in 2000 — halving Europe's measurable trade chokepoints in a quarter century.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Sets a decay rate on EU trade leverage: any European escalation strategy has a shrinking asset base, which argues for front-loading rather than sequencing pressure.
insights.locator: MERICS research shows that the number of product categories

insights.claim: China's pursuit of economic self-sufficiency is the identified cause of the steady decline in its reliance on European imports, with import substitution through domestic production expected to reduce dependencies further.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: European industrial exporters into China face structural, policy-driven share loss regardless of tariffs — a secular derating risk for EU capital-goods and pharma exposure.
insights.quote: China’s pursuit of economic self-sufficiency is steadily reducing the country’s reliance on European imports.
insights.locator: At the same time, MERICS data also suggests

insights.claim: Even Germany's individual trade leverage over China has become marginal, with China's dependencies on German products dropping to nine HS6 categories from twelve over the 2000-2024 period.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Berlin has almost no unilateral bargaining chip left with Beijing, undercutting the German business lobby's case for bilateral accommodation over EU-level action.
insights.locator: even Germany’s individual contribution has become more marginal

insights.claim: China depends on the EU for roughly twice as many types of products as on the US, relying on the US for only 56 HS6 categories in 2024 against the EU's 110.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Contradicts the assumption that Washington holds all the coercive cards — Europe's breadth of leverage is greater even if its depth in semis is not.
insights.locator: China still depends on EU imports for many more products

insights.claim: Of more than 300 HS6 categories MERICS identifies as crucial for economic or national security, China depended on the EU for 15 in 2024 — including hormones and steroids, alkaloids used in pharma and pesticides, vaccines, zirconium, gas turbines, certain machine tools, and helicopters and airplanes.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Names the specific European industries that would be weaponized or targeted in an EU-China trade conflict — a concrete watchlist for export-control and retaliation risk.
insights.locator: In the absence of a universally accepted catalogue

insights.claim: China relied on the US for only three strategic products in 2024 — two borates used in nuclear coolants and fiberglass, plus airplanes — a far narrower strategic grip than Europe's fifteen.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: US leverage over China in customs-visible strategic goods is thin, meaning American pressure depends disproportionately on export controls outside HS6 categories.
insights.locator: In contrast, China relied on the US for only three strategic products

insights.claim: Excluding non-essential goods like wigs and focusing on strategic goods such as pharmaceuticals makes Europe's leverage position look even stronger relative to the US.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Headline dependency counts understate Europe's real hand — pharma is the sector where EU pressure would bite hardest.
insights.locator: Excluding non-essential goods like wigs

insights.claim: HS6 customs codes are too coarse to capture real chokepoints: Chinese imports of cutting-edge US semiconductors are grouped with widely made legacy chips, and crucial Dutch semiconductor lithography machines are subsumed within broader, less critical categories.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Any dependency ranking built on customs data systematically undercounts the highest-value tech chokepoints — adjust before using these counts to size escalation risk.
insights.quote: Chinese imports of cutting-edge US semiconductors, for example, are grouped with widely made legacy chips.
insights.locator: Admittedly, HS6 codes are not granular enough

insights.claim: The undercounting from coarse customs categories applies symmetrically to Europe and the US, so the EU-versus-US comparison of dependency breadth still holds despite the data's limits.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Defends the relative conclusion even where absolute counts are wrong — the asymmetry finding is robust enough to trade policy expectations on.
insights.quote: But this undercounting applies to Europe as well
insights.locator: But this undercounting applies to Europe as well

insights.claim: MERICS defines import dependency by three simultaneous criteria — imports at least twice exports, one partner supplying at least 30 percent of imports, and market concentration with an HHI of 0.25 or higher — using BACI data from CEPII built on UN Comtrade.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: The exact thresholds matter: dependency counts are sensitive to the 30 percent and 0.25 cutoffs, so cross-study comparisons need the same definition.
insights.locator: Methodology

insights.claim: EU import dependencies on China appear to have peaked, falling from 422 product categories in 2022 to 411 in 2024 after years of expansion.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: First hard evidence that EU derisking is showing up in customs data, though an 11-category decline off 422 is marginal — treat the turning point as tentative.
insights.quote: this trend appears to have reached a tipping point
insights.locator: Europe is finally reducing its own reliance on China

insights.claim: The EU's strategic dependencies on China peaked at 20 categories in 2022 and dropped only slightly to 19 in 2024, still including graphite, fluorspar, some antibiotics, amino compounds and heterocyclic compounds used as pharmaceutical precursors.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: These five categories are Europe's live vulnerability list and the most probable targets of Chinese retaliation — supply-chain and pricing risk for EU battery and generic-pharma chains.
insights.locator: Similarly, the number of the EU’s strategic dependencies

insights.claim: Rare earths are less concentrated than commonly assumed: while the EU imported a large share from China, BACI data show Australia and Vietnam were also major exporters, reducing global market concentration.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Cuts against the consensus rare-earth chokehold narrative for the EU specifically — a reason to be selective about rare-earth scarcity trades.
insights.locator: (The EU imported a large share of rare earths from China

themes.theme: Policy tooling: ACI and sourcing rules

insights.claim: MERICS argues that if the EU wants to exploit its leverage in a trade conflict with China the time to act is now, because Beijing's import substitution will keep eroding those dependencies.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Frames EU-China escalation as time-sensitive, raising the probability of European trade measures in the near term rather than after further study.
insights.quote: if the EU wants to exploit its leverage in a trade conflict with China, the time to do so is now
insights.locator: First, if the EU wants to exploit its leverage

insights.claim: The Anti-Coercion Instrument can currently be activated only after lengthy EU Council approval and a formal request for the coercing country to stop, so letting the Commission act on its own would make the EU's threat to restrict exports credible.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Watch for proposals to give the Commission autonomous ACI authority — that institutional change, not new tariffs, is what would repriced EU-China escalation risk.
insights.locator: The Anti-Coercion Instrument (ACI) is the EU’s principal tool

insights.claim: Brussels is already considering a local sourcing requirement that would oblige companies in sensitive sectors to maintain at least three different sources of critical supplies.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: A three-source mandate would force duplicate qualification spending across EU industrials and create demand for non-Chinese suppliers in critical inputs.
insights.locator: One option is a local sourcing requirement

insights.claim: Going on a trade offensive would require the EU to get more serious about defense in the form of economic derisking, since escalation exposes remaining European dependencies to retaliation.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Sequencing matters: an EU offensive without completed derisking invites asymmetric Chinese retaliation in graphite, fluorspar and pharma precursors.
insights.quote: Were the EU to go on a trade offensive, it would need to get more serious about defense – namely, economic derisking – as well.
insights.locator: Were the EU to go on a trade offensive

insights.claim: Collective EU action is far more likely to deter China than any single member state acting alone, which makes German alignment with a common strategy a precondition rather than a nicety.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: EU-China trade risk hinges on internal cohesion — track German positioning as the leading indicator of whether Brussels can actually escalate.
insights.quote: if the EU acts collectively, it has a much better chance of deterring China than any one country on its own
insights.locator: Germany needs to fall in line with a common EU strategy

insights.claim: Germany's traditionally cooperative approach and its footdragging over tougher trade measures risk undermining the EU's collective deterrence, but Berlin's July plan to revive the German economy called for protection against unfair competition and faster, sector-wide anti-dumping and anti-subsidy measures at European level.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: A concrete German policy shift toward faster sector-wide trade defense raises the odds of EU duties landing on more Chinese sectors than EVs.
insights.locator: But Berlin appears to have recognized that

insights.claim: European companies are being threatened out of business by a flood of state-subsidized Chinese imports while Brussels negotiates, in contrast to Washington's aggressive use of chokepoints such as high-end semiconductors to extract Chinese trade concessions.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: The implicit recommendation is that Europe copy the US coercive playbook — a regime shift that would raise tail risk for EU-listed China-exposed industrials both ways.
insights.quote: But while Washington has aggressively leveraged its so-called chokepoints – for example, in high-end semiconductors – to secure Chinese trade concessions

insights.claim: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen used her September 2023 State of the EU address to announce the anti-subsidy probe into Chinese electric vehicles, the reference point for how EU trade offensives have been launched.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Precedent suggests set-piece political speeches, not technical filings, are the trigger points to watch for the next sectoral probe.
insights.locator: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen used her annual State of the EU address
